extracted.intended_audience: EPA rulewriters and regulatory staff; policymakers; public commenters and environmental advocates
extracted.subtask_short: EPA residual risk review for oil and gas
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and recommended criteria for how EPA should assess and determine acceptable cancer, acute, and chronic non-cancer risks for the Oil and Gas Production and Natural Gas Transmission and Storage source categories under CAA section 112(f)(2). Focuses on cumulative exposures, vulnerable populations, and updating presumptive risk thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider net burden of exposures (not single-chemical focus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Risk assessments must consider the net burden of exposures to chemicals and not be limited to one chemical at a time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites EPA Risk Assessment Guidance for Superfund which provides for consideration of net burden and has been implemented for more than a decade; implies evaluators should aggregate exposures rather than assessing pollutants in isolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for mixtures of chemical agents
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must be able to consider mixtures of chemical agents when looking at public health concerns because no one is exposed only to single agents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt research and modeling approaches to better understand dose-response relationships for chemical mixtures and follow related EPA guidelines and methods development for mixtures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address cumulative impacts and community-based risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Risk assessment must address cumulative impacts and community-based risks to public health from multiple sources and exposures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses EPA Framework for Cumulative Risk Assessment and NRC reports; recommends evaluating risk from a community health perspective and incorporating cumulative risk literature and methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate children’s unique vulnerability and early-life exposures
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessments must account for the greater health risks created by early exposure to toxic pollution and recognize that children are not little adults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate childhood and prenatal exposure analyses, use child-specific reference doses (e.g., California child-specific reference doses), follow EPA guidance on considering children’s health (EO 13045 and EPA ADP Guide).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider biomonitoring and toxic body burden evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Risk assessments should reflect the increased scientific knowledge about chemicals present in human bodies and the significance of toxic body burden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites CDC biomonitoring (Fourth National Report) showing many chemicals in people’s bodies and argues this information should inform standards and protection levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor environmental justice into acceptability determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA’s commitment to environmental justice must inform what level of risk is considered 'acceptable.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply EPA’s EJ definition (fair treatment and meaningful involvement), factor Plan EJ 2014 and SAB work into rulemaking, and ensure decisions protect communities that disproportionately bear pollution burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reassess and update presumptive acceptable lifetime cancer risk
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA should not presume that any lifetime cancer risk below 100-in-1 million remains acceptable; EPA must reassess whether a level closer to the statutory aspirational goal of 1-in-1 million should be the presumptive upper limit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contemporary science, technology, and social values have changed since the Benzene Rule; EPA must perform updated assessments, consider community-level acceptability, and justify any decision to retain higher presumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not treat Benzene Rule presumptions as permanent or insulating
rubrics_metrics.description: References to the Benzene Rule do not authorize EPA to freeze its approach or avoid strengthening residual risk methods in light of changed circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal and legislative history support EPA authority and responsibility to update approaches; the 1990 CAA amendments intended stronger protections, not perpetuation of old presumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide reasoned justification when not reducing acute health risks above HQ>1
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must explain and justify any decision not to reduce acute health risk when calculated hazard quotients substantially exceed the HQ threshold of 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA found HQs up to 9 (benzene) and 3 (glycol ethers) but offered unsupported rationales; agency must address why such high HQs would be safe or acceptable given uncertainties and analysis flaws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on AEGL/ERPG values for residual risk determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Acute Exposure Guideline Levels (AEGLs) and ERPGs, developed for emergency exposures, are inappropriate for section 112(f)(2) residual risk assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AEGL/ERPG are for once-in-a-lifetime or emergency releases and may underestimate chronic or repeated short-term exposures; instead use RELs or community-protective reference exposure levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not discount high acute risk due to small exposed populations
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must not perform triage by deeming high risks acceptable because only a small number of people are exposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the most-exposed individuals face unacceptable risk (e.g., people living within 2 miles), EPA has a duty to require reductions; agency must justify any geographic or population cutoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sum acute health risks across pollutants and sources (create acute TOSHI)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA should aggregate acute health risks across pollutants affecting the same organ/system (analogous to TOSHI for chronic risk) and consider contributions from outside the source category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA did not sum acute risks and only considered maximum single-pollutant HQs; failure to aggregate understates risk to organ systems and individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use community reference exposure levels (RELs), not occupational limits, for residents
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA should not substitute occupational short-term exposure limits (STEL) for community resident reference exposure levels when evaluating acute/community risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occupational standards protect workers for limited durations and are not protective for lifetime community exposures; RELs intended for community exposure are more appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not presume chronic non-cancer risk is safe at HQ/TOSHI ≤ 1 without support
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA’s presumption that a hazard quotient or TOSHI of 1 or below indicates safety is unsupported and must be justified or revised downward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The agency’s own 2002 staff memo recommended a default HI limit well under 1 (e.g., 0.2) to account for multiple sources; HQ=1 is merely EPA’s presumption and is arbitrary without record support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt a presumptive chronic non-cancer contribution limit of 0.2 (or lower)
rubrics_metrics.description: For section 112(f)(2) determinations, EPA should set a presumptive limit on a source category’s TOSHI contribution at no higher than 0.2 (and in some communities 0.1) to protect against cumulative exposures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 2002 Residual Risk Program memo rationale: 0.2 allows a single source to account for up to 20% of total exposure and avoids allowing one source to dominate total exposures; in heavily impacted communities an even lower cutoff is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate total individual exposure from multiple nearby sources
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must evaluate an individual's total exposure to HAPs (from the source category plus other facilities and sources) when assessing non-cancer risks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that pollutant-specific RfCs are threshold-based; exposures from multiple sources may combine to cause increased risk even if any single source is below concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not ignore facility-wide high TOSHI based on arbitrary percentage cutoffs
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA should not dismiss high facility-wide chronic non-cancer risks by using an arbitrary cutoff (e.g., 50% contribution) to decide whether a source 'drives' facility risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even contributions below 50% may be significant enough to warrant controls; EPA must explain and justify any significance thresholds and provide transparency about sources included in facility-wide analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for emissions from malfunctions, violations, and real-world worst-cases
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA’s worst-case assumptions (e.g., a factor of 10 multiplier) are inadequate if they omit malfunctions or violations; risk estimates must adequately capture realistic peak emissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA’s acute risk factor of 10 may not reflect true worst-case; agency must include malfunction scenarios and not undercount peak emissions that drive acute exposures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not arbitrarily limit spatial scope of exposure analysis (e.g., 2-mile radius)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must justify and, where appropriate, expand the geographic radius used to assess community exposures rather than relying on an unexplained 2-mile cutoff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expanding analysis to larger radii will better protect those who may face slightly lower but still meaningful acute or chronic risks; EPA must justify any chosen boundary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess acceptable risk using contemporary science, technology, and social values at local level
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must make acceptability determinations 'in the world in which we live' by taking into account modern science, technologies, and evolved societal views — including community perspectives on acceptable risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given changes since the Benzene presumption, EPA should reassess acceptable levels (toward the 1-in-1 million aspirational goal), perform updated evaluations, and consider what a local community would view as acceptable.
